overview: This layer shows the Republic of Malta during the map’s 1994 to 2020 coverage. The republic was already established: independence came in 1964 and republican government in 1974. Malta, Gozo and the smaller islands form a Mediterranean archipelago whose households combine local language and traditions with close international connections. Neither endpoint marks the creation or disappearance of the country.

periods.title: A republic debating European membership
periods.summary: Malta considered its relationship with the European Union through elections, negotiations and a referendum.

periods.title: European Union membership
periods.summary: Membership began in 2004, followed by the euro changeover in 2008 and further changes in public services.

sections.title: Government and a changing pocketful of coins

items.text: Malta’s route into the European Union was debated rather than automatic. Its application was paused in 1996 and reactivated after the 1998 election. Negotiations began in 2000, and a referendum in 2003 supported joining. Malta became a member on 1 May 2004.

The euro replaced the Maltese lira on 1 January 2008. To prepare, banks received new notes and coins before the changeover, and the public could buy small starter kits from 10 December 2007. People could examine their new coins before using them for ordinary shopping.

For January 2008, payments could be made in either euros or Maltese lira notes and coins. The overlap ended on 31 January. This short transition gave households and shops time to adjust, rather than requiring everyone to empty every old coin from every drawer overnight.

Malta is a parliamentary republic with one chamber of parliament. The prime minister heads the government, while the president’s role is largely ceremonial. Distinguishing these jobs helps explain why a national ceremony and the day-to-day work of governing can involve different people.

Ftira is a flattened sourdough bread with a firm crust and an airy inside. A split loaf can hold olive oil, tomato, tuna, capers or olives. UNESCO added its associated knowledge and customs to its heritage list in 2020. Here a much-loved lunch also carries a history of skilled work.

Ftira still needs skilled hands to shape it, even where other bread-making jobs use machines. Apprentices learn by watching and doing. At home, people pass on ideas for fillings, while cooking blogs and social media also share variations. A recipe can travel between generations and between screens.

A 2018 European research report describes grandparents as important carers for many Maltese children under three. It also notes expanding childcare provision and more mothers of young children in paid work. Family care could involve several generations as well as services outside the home.

The same report describes football, ballet and clubs among children’s activities after school. In the Maltese families studied, digital reading coexisted with valued printed books, and many parents worried about internet safety. The findings concern a research sample, giving a glimpse of family life rather than a rule for every home.

Three new wastewater plants changed what happened after toilets were flushed. Plants in Gozo and northern Malta began operating in 2007 and 2008; Ta’ Barkat followed in June 2011. The environment authority describes this programme as a way to stop raw sewage being discharged into the sea.

Moving into Mater Dei Hospital in November 2007 required a carefully coordinated transfer from St Luke’s. The official report records 411 acute patients and nine babies moved during the process. Some non-acute patients stayed behind. Opening a hospital meant moving people safely as well as unlocking a new building.

Blood donation also went out into the community. The transfusion service records 206 blood drives in 2008, including visits to clinics and factories, collecting 3,124 units. A refurbished mobile unit was inaugurated in 2009. Ordinary volunteers helped provide something that hospitals could not simply manufacture.

Village festas bring volunteers, bands, bells and street food together. UNESCO’s later 2023 account explains that preparation continues through the year and that some parishes hold children’s processions with a smaller statue. These continuing celebrations give children ways to participate, rather than only watching the grown-ups.

Article 5 of the Maltese constitution reads: “L-ilsien Nazzjonali ta’ Malta huwa l-ilsien Malti.” It means “The National language of Malta is the Maltese language.” This quotation follows the government’s 2019 printed text. The following paragraph also identifies Maltese and English as official languages, showing how language is part of public life as well as family conversation.

ending.text: The map stops at 2020, but the Republic of Malta continues. It remains a parliamentary republic and a member of the European Union. Its later history belongs to continuing communities rather than an ending civilisation.
